result:
Neither. The premise is the problem: more agents do not always give better results.

Every extra agent costs you something:
- **Money.** Each agent re-reads its own instructions and context, and agents pass long messages to each other. Anthropic reported that its multi-agent research system used about 15 times the tokens of a plain chat. Your sponsor's budget is small, so this matters.
- **Hand-off errors.** Each time one agent summarizes for another, details can get lost.
- **Harder debugging.** With ten agents, you can't easily tell which one caused a wrong booking.

Here is a concrete example from your assistant. A student asks: "Can I book the laser cutter Thursday at 2?" One agent can search the manual for the training requirements, check the calendar, and book the slot. That is three tool calls in one loop. Splitting it into a manual agent, a calendar agent and a booking agent adds two hand-offs and gains nothing.

Splitting starts to pay off when the work is large, can run in parallel, or would overflow one context window. Reading hundreds of manual pages at once is an example. Your assistant's requests are small and sequential, so a single agent is probably enough.

My suggestion is to start with one agent with well-described tools. Make any fixed steps, such as "always check the calendar before booking", a plain workflow in code. Add a second agent only when you can name a specific failure that one agent can't handle. Then your design review has a reason to point to.

Quick check: for the Thursday request, which steps would you make fixed code, and which would you leave to the model?

I can turn this into a lesson on workflows versus agents and when multi-agent pays off. Just ask.
